paragraphs.heading: One element makes everything
paragraphs.text: A cyclic group is a group generated by a single element. That means the group holds some element g, and every other element comes from applying the group operation to g, or to the inverse of g, over and over. Each element can then be written as an integer power of g, or as an integer multiple of g when the operation is written as addition. The element g is called a generator of the group.

paragraphs.heading: Integers and remainders
paragraphs.text: The integers Z under addition form a cyclic group with no end: every integer can be reached by adding or subtracting 1 again and again. Only 1 and −1 can serve as generators of it. For any positive integer n, the integers modulo n under addition form a finite cyclic group, written Z/nZ. Every infinite cyclic group is isomorphic to Z, and a finite cyclic group with n elements is isomorphic to Z/nZ.

paragraphs.heading: Powers become sums
paragraphs.text: Matching a cyclic group with Z/nZ sends the identity element to 0, products to sums and powers to multiples. For example, with n = 6, the sum 1 + 2 ≡ 3 (mod 6) matches the product z¹ · z² = z³. In Z/nZ, a number i is a generator when i is relatively prime to n. How many such generators there are is given by φ(n), the Euler totient function.

paragraphs.heading: Always commutative
paragraphs.text: Every cyclic group is abelian, meaning its group operation is commutative. Going the other way, any abelian group with finitely many generators is a direct product of cyclic groups. A cyclic group of prime order is a simple group, so it cannot be broken down into smaller groups. In the classification of finite simple groups, these prime-order cyclic groups form one of the three infinite classes, which makes them among the building blocks of all groups.

paragraphs.heading: Turning shapes
paragraphs.text: The rotational symmetries of a polygon form a finite cyclic group. If a polygon can be rotated onto itself in n different ways, counting the null rotation, this group is isomorphic to Z/nZ. The rotations of a whole circle, called the circle group S¹, do not form a cyclic group: no single rotation has integer powers that reach every rotation. Even the rotations by rational angles, though countable, are still not cyclic.

paragraphs.heading: Roots of unity
paragraphs.text: A complex number that gives 1 when raised to the nth power is called an nth root of unity. Taken together, all the nth roots of unity form a cyclic group of order n under multiplication. Its generators are the primitive nth roots of unity, which are the roots of the nth cyclotomic polynomial.

paragraphs.heading: A name that can mislead
paragraphs.text: Some groups with one generator have no finite cycles at all, such as the first frieze group, so the word "cyclic" can mislead. To sidestep the confusion, Bourbaki brought in the term monogenous group for any group with a single generator. Bourbaki kept "cyclic group" for the finite ones and avoided saying "infinite cyclic group".
